title: Tell me about a time you went above and beyond for a customer or user
prompt: Tell me about a time you made a useful extra effort to understand and help a customer, user, learner or another person you supported. Explain their need, what you did within your responsibilities, and what changed. Qualitative outcomes are welcome; business revenue is not required.
blurb: Customer obsession: did they dig into the real customer need and act on it — or just perform helpfulness?

rubric.label: Customer & their real need
rubric.description: Explains the person’s actual need, how it was understood and any relevant constraints without assuming that the initial request captures the whole problem.

rubric.label: Why they went further
rubric.description: Explains the candidate’s responsibility and reason for helping, whether self-initiated or part of an assigned duty; unpaid or out-of-scope work is not required.

rubric.label: Specific contribution and decisions
rubric.description: Describes a specific helpful action, checks understanding and stays within authorization, consent and safety boundaries.

rubric.label: Outcome and evidence
rubric.description: Describes a supported qualitative or quantitative outcome for the person or service and any tradeoff; revenue or profit is not required.

rubric.label: Reflection & generalization
rubric.description: Identifies a useful lesson or proportionate improvement that could help in a similar situation; a wider rollout is not mandatory.

rubric.label: Clear, relevant communication
rubric.description: Makes the relevant situation, reasoning and contribution understandable in any clear order. No required STAR structure, pronouns, performance of confidence or emotional tone.

reference.scenario: Explore attentive service to a customer, learner, community member or another person receiving support. The context may be commercial, educational, public or nonprofit. Assess understanding, useful action, safe boundaries and the person’s outcome rather than business value or heroics.
model_points: Explains who needed help and how the candidate checked what mattered to them.
Distinguishes the request from the underlying need without assuming the person was wrong.
Takes an appropriate action or arranges qualified help within their role.
Balances the person’s needs with safety, consent, available resources and fairness to others.
Describes what changed for the person using honest qualitative or quantitative evidence; no commercial metric is necessary.
Identifies a lesson, a small process change or when the same approach would not fit.

probes.trigger: the underlying need is assumed rather than checked
probes.question: How did you check what mattered most to that person?

probes.trigger: the action may exceed the candidate’s responsibility
probes.question: How did you check that this was within your role?
What changed for the person after your action?

red_flags: Promises an outcome or benefit they know they cannot authorize.
Ignores stated consent, safety or privacy boundaries to appear helpful.
Claims the person benefited despite evidence in their own account that the need remained unresolved.
follow_ups: What would you adapt if another person had a similar need?
How did you account for other people waiting for help?
reference.exemplar_answer: Illustrative example only; it is not a required setting, answer order or achievement standard. At a library volunteer desk, someone asked me to fill out a private online form for them. I checked what help they needed and explained that I could show the navigation without handling their private answers. With their agreement, I used a blank example and stayed available for general questions. They completed the form themselves. I suggested a short navigation guide so future visitors could use the same support.
reference.assessment_contract: Assess the selected competency from concrete job-relevant evidence. Examples from paid work, study, volunteering, caregiving, informal work, military service and community activities are equally eligible when relevant. A modest example is sufficient if it shows the competency; employer prestige, formal title and financial scale are not criteria. Accept qualitative or quantitative outcomes supported by the account, including partial or unsuccessful outcomes. Do not require a numeric metric, STAR order, particular pronouns, composure, enthusiasm or a particular communication style. Identify personal contribution by meaning while preserving credit to others. Assess intelligibility and relevance, not accent, fluency, verbosity, visible emotion, disability or private circumstances. Mark genuinely missing evidence not assessed; do not infer poor competence or dishonesty from an absent example. A clearly labeled hypothetical may be discussed as situational practice but must not count as demonstrated past experience. Respect scope of practice, authorization, safety and ethical duties; pausing, declining, reporting or escalating can be sound judgment. Never require obedience, direct confrontation, unpaid overwork or successful persuasion regardless of the circumstances.
